claim: The Eph receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) family is the largest subfamily of RTKs.
source: The Eph receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) family is the largest subfamily of RTKs playing critical roles in many developmental processes such as tissue patterning, neurogenesis and neuronal circuit formation, angiogenesis, etc.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Eph receptors play critical roles in tissue patterning, neurogenesis and neuronal circuit formation, and angiogenesis.
source: The Eph receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) family is the largest subfamily of RTKs playing critical roles in many developmental processes such as tissue patterning, neurogenesis and neuronal circuit formation, angiogenesis, etc.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: There are 14 Eph proteins in mammals.
source: How the 14 Eph proteins, via their highly similar cytoplasmic domains, can transmit diverse and sometimes opposite cellular signals upon engaging ephrins is a major unresolved question.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of all 14 Eph receptors are highly similar.
source: However, the cytoplasmic portion of all 14 Eph receptors are highly similar, each containing a membrane-juxtaposing kinase domain, a protein-binding SAM domain immediately followed by a short carboxyl tail PDZ domain-binding motif (PBM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Each Eph receptor cytoplasmic domain contains a membrane-juxtaposing kinase domain, a protein-binding SAM domain, and a short carboxyl tail PDZ domain-binding motif (PBM).
source: However, the cytoplasmic portion of all 14 Eph receptors are highly similar, each containing a membrane-juxtaposing kinase domain, a protein-binding SAM domain immediately followed by a short carboxyl tail PDZ domain-binding motif (PBM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The study systematically investigated the bindings of each SAM domain of Eph receptors to the SAM domains from SHIP2 and Odin.
source: Here, we systematically investigated the bindings of each SAM domain of Eph receptors to the SAM domains from SHIP2 and Odin, and uncover a highly specific SAM–SAM interaction-mediated cytoplasmic Eph-effector binding pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The study uncovered a highly specific SAM–SAM interaction-mediated cytoplasmic Eph-effector binding pattern.
source: Here, we systematically investigated the bindings of each SAM domain of Eph receptors to the SAM domains from SHIP2 and Odin, and uncover a highly specific SAM–SAM interaction-mediated cytoplasmic Eph-effector binding pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The study identified SAMD5 as a new Eph binding partner.
source: Finally, these Eph/effector SAM heterodimer structures can explain many Eph SAM mutations identified in patients suffering from cancers and other diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The Eph receptor superfamily contains 14 members in mammals.
source: The Eph (erythropoietin-producing hepatocyte) transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase superfamily, with its first member identified30 years ago (Hirai et al., 1987), contains 14 members in mammals and is the largest among all receptor tyrosine kinase families (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010; Manning et al., 2002; Murai and Pasquale, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The first member of the Eph receptor family was identified 30 years ago.
source: The Eph (erythropoietin-producing hepatocyte) transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase superfamily, with its first member identified30 years ago (Hirai et al., 1987), contains 14 members in mammals and is the largest among all receptor tyrosine kinase families (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010; Manning et al., 2002; Murai and Pasquale, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Hirai et al., 1987.

claim: Eph receptors are classified into the EphA and EphB subfamilies based on their engaging ephrin ligands.
source: Chiefly based on their engaging ephrin ligands, Eph receptors are classified into the EphA and EphB subfamilies, each with nine and five members in mammals, respectively (Eph Nomenclature Committee , 1997; Gale et al., 1996; Murai and Pasquale, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The EphA subfamily has nine members in mammals.
source: Chiefly based on their engaging ephrin ligands, Eph receptors are classified into the EphA and EphB subfamilies, each with nine and five members in mammals, respectively (Eph Nomenclature Committee , 1997; Gale et al., 1996; Murai and Pasquale, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The EphB subfamily has five members in mammals.
source: Chiefly based on their engaging ephrin ligands, Eph receptors are classified into the EphA and EphB subfamilies, each with nine and five members in mammals, respectively (Eph Nomenclature Committee , 1997; Gale et al., 1996; Murai and Pasquale, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Ephrin-Eph signaling regulates stem cell maintenance and differentiations, tissue morphogenesis, and tissue–tissue boundary formation.
source: Owing to broad expressions in essentially all tissues and at every life stage, Ephrin-Eph signaling regulates many cellular processes both during development and in developed animals such as stem cell maintenance and differentiations, tissue morphogenesis, and tissue–tissue boundary formation (Batlle and Wilkinson, 2012; Genander and Frisén, 2010; Jülich et al., 2009; McMillen and Holley, 2015; Munarini et al., 2002; Park et al., 2011; Poliakov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations of ephrins and Ephs cause many forms of diseases including cancers and brain disorders.
source: Not surprisingly, mutations of ephrins and Ephs are known to cause many forms of diseases including cancers and brain disorders (Boyd et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2008; Hahn et al., 2012; Kania and Klein, 2016; Merlos-Suárez and Batlle, 2008; Pasquale, 2008; Zhuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Ephrin ligand binding-mediated inter-cellular signaling is the classic mode of Eph receptor signaling.
source: Ephrin ligand binding-mediated inter-cellular signaling is the classic mode of Eph receptor signaling (also known as ephrin-Eph 'forward' signaling), which is responsible for the majority of cellular functions characterized for the ephrin-Eph signaling (Pitulescu and Adams, 2010; Taylor et al., 2017; Yokoyama et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Ephrin-A5 binds to EphA2 and EphA4 with similar affinity but induces cell adhesion or cell collapse, respectively.
source: For example, ephrin-A5 binds to EphA2 and EphA4 with similar affinity but induces cell adhesion or cell collapse, respectively (Cooper et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2007), although different multimerization modes of EphA2 and EphA4 extracellular domains induced by ephrin-A5 binding can also contribute to the opposite cell spreading phenotype (Seiradake et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: SHIP2 is a mammalian inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase.
source: SHIP2 is a mammalian inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases and is the only member in the family that contains a C-terminal SAM domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: SHIP2 is the only member in the inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase family that contains a C-terminal SAM domain.
source: SHIP2 is a mammalian inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases and is the only member in the family that contains a C-terminal SAM domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SHIP2 was reported to be a binding partner of EphA2 through SAM–SAM interaction.
source: It has been reported that SHIP2 was a binding partner of EphA2 through SAM–SAM interaction (Lee et al., 2012; Leone et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: EphA2 SAM and SHIP2 SAM each behave as homogeneous monomers in solution.
source: Both Eph SAM and SHIP2 SAM alone behaved as homogeneous monomers in solution as indicated by the analytical gel filtration analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A 1:1 mixture of EphA2 SAM and SHIP2 SAM forms a hetero SAM-SAM complex.
source: While the 1:1 mixture of EphA2 SAM and SHIP2 SAM was eluted at a smaller volume than the individual proteins, suggesting the formation of a hetero SAM-SAM complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: EphA2 SAM binds to SHIP2 SAM with a dissociation constant (Kd) of ~2.22 μM at a 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: ITC (Isothermal Titration Calorimetry) experiment revealed that EphA2 SAM bound to SHIP2 SAM with a dissociation constant (Kd) of ~2.22 μM at a 1:1 stoichiometry (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only the SAM domains of EphA1/EphA2/EphA6 specifically bind to SHIP2 SAM.
source: We found that only the SAM domains of EphA1/EphA2/EphA6 specifically bound to SHIP2 SAM, and the rest of Eph SAM domains displayed no detectable binding to SHIP2 SAM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Odin was reported to be a binding partner of EphA2.
source: Odin was reported to be another binding partner of EphA2 (Kim et al., 2010; Mercurio et al., 2012), and the interaction had been implicated in affecting the stability of EphA2 by modulating its ubiquitination process (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The interaction between Odin and EphA2 affects the stability of EphA2 by modulating its ubiquitination process.
source: Odin was reported to be another binding partner of EphA2 (Kim et al., 2010; Mercurio et al., 2012), and the interaction had been implicated in affecting the stability of EphA2 by modulating its ubiquitination process (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Odin SAM1 only selectively binds to the SAM domains from EphA1/EphA2/EphA6.
source: The results showed that, similar to SHIP2 SAM, Odin SAM1 only selectively bound to the SAM domains from EphA1/EphA2/EphA6 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The interactions between Eph SAMs and their downstream effectors are highly specific.
source: The quantitative and systematic binding results shown in Figure 1D indicated that the interactions between Eph SAMs and their downstream effectors were highly specific.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The crystal structure of the SHIP2 SAM-EphA2 SAM complex was determined at 1.5 Å resolution.
source: To elucidate the molecular mechanism governing the specificity of the bindings of SHIP2 SAM and Odin SAM1 to Eph receptors, we determined the crystal structure of the SHIP2 SAM-EphA2 SAM complex and the Odin SAM1-EphA6 SAM complex at the 1.5 Å and 1.3 Å resolutions, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Table 1.

claim: The crystal structure of the Odin SAM1-EphA6 SAM complex was determined at 1.3 Å resolution.
source: To elucidate the molecular mechanism governing the specificity of the bindings of SHIP2 SAM and Odin SAM1 to Eph receptors, we determined the crystal structure of the SHIP2 SAM-EphA2 SAM complex and the Odin SAM1-EphA6 SAM complex at the 1.5 Å and 1.3 Å resolutions, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Table 1.

claim: The EphA2/SHIP2 and EphA6/Odin complex structures adopt an essentially identical End-Helix/Mid-Loop binding mode.
source: The two complex structures adopt an essentially identical End-Helix/Mid-Loop binding mode, in which positively charged residues from the N-terminal end of α5 (End-Helix) of EphA2/EphA6 bind to negatively charged residues from the loop connecting α2-α4 (Mid-Loop) from SHIP2/Odin, forming the well-known tail-to-head SAM domain heterodimer (Figure 2A–E) (Qiao and Bowie, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A-E.

claim: The backbone methylene of Gly954A2/Gly1104A6 is in close contact with Trp1221SHIP2/Phe738Odin.
source: A noticeable feature in both complexes is that the backbone methylene of a Gly residue at the beginning of α5 from Eph SAM (Gly954A2/Gly1104A6) is in close contact with an aromatic residue from SHIP2/Odin SAM (Trp1221SHIP2/Phe738Odin) (Figure 2B and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B, D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Replacing Gly at the beginning of α5 of Eph SAM with any other amino acid residues will introduce steric hindrance preventing binding to SHIP2/Odin SAM.
source: As such, replacing Gly at the beginning of α5 of Eph SAM with any other amino acid residues will introduce steric hindrance in preventing their binding to SHIP2/Odin SAM.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: Gly is highly preferred at the beginning of α5 among Eph SAM domains (12 out of 14 members).
source: It is further noted that Gly is highly preferred at the beginning of α5 among Eph SAM domains (12 out of the 14 members are Gly; see Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: A special cation-π interaction between Arg958A2 and Phe1226SHIP2 is critical for the specific interaction between EphA2 SAM and SHIP2 SAM.
source: The very high-resolution crystal structures of the two complexes also allowed us to identify a unique interaction feature that is critical for the exquisite specific interaction between the EphA2/A6 SAM domain and SHIP2/Odin SAM domains. Taking the EphA2/SHIP2 complex as the example, a special cation-π interaction between the Arg958A2 and Phe1226SHIP2 was uncovered by the high-resolution crystal structure (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The guanidinium group of Arg958A2 forms a hydrogen bond network with Asp1222SHIP2 and His955A2 on one side and with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Ile917A2.
source: The guanidinium group of Arg958A2 forms hydrogen bond network with Asp1222SHIP2 and His955A2 on one side and with the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Ile917A2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The guanidinium plane of Arg958A2 forms energetically favorable π-π stacking with the benzene ring of Phe1226SHIP2.
source: As such the guanidinium plane of Arg958A2 (and its delocalized π-system) is in the same plane with the π-system of the planer peptide bond between Ile917A2 and Lys918A2, forming energetically favorable π-π stacking with the benzene ring of Phe1226SHIP2 (Figure 2F) (Ma and Dougherty, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F with a supporting citation.

claim: Substitution of Arg958A2 with Lys completely eliminated the bindings of EphA2 SAM to SHIP2 SAM or Odin SAM.
source: Totally consistent with this structural analysis, substitution of Arg958A2 with Lys completely eliminated the bindings of EphA2 SAM to SHIP2 SAM or Odin SAM (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: Substitution of Phe1226 of SHIP2 SAM with Leu or Ala totally eliminated the binding between SHIP2 SAM and EphA2 SAM.
source: Correspondingly, substitution of Phe1226 of SHIP2 SAM with non-aromatic hydrophobic residues (e.g. Leu or Ala) also totally eliminated the binding between SHIP2 SAM and EphA2 SAM (Figure 2H and J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H and J.

claim: Replacing Asp1222 in SHIP2 SAM with Ala eliminated the binding between SHIP2 and EphA2.
source: Additionally, replacing Asp1222 in SHIP2 SAM with Ala also eliminated the binding between SHIP2 and EphA2, highlighting the importance of the hydrogen bond between Asp1222SHIP2 and Arg958A2 in stabilizing the guanidinium group of Arg958 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: An Arg957 to Cys somatic mutation of EphA2 has been detected in ovary carcinoma patients.
source: We mined COSMIC cancer somatic mutation database (Forbes et al., 2017; http://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic) and found that an Arg957 (corresponding to mouse Arg958) to Cys somatic mutation of EphA2 has been detected in ovary carcinoma patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the COSMIC database.

claim: Substitution of Arg with Cys in EphA2 completely eliminated EphA2 SAM's binding to SHIP2 or Odin.
source: As expected, substitution of Arg with Cys also completely eliminated EphA2 SAM's binding to the SHIP2 or Odin (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: Substituting Lys857 of EphA5 SAM with Arg converted EphA5 SAM into a SHIP2 binding SAM domain.
source: Satisfyingly, substituting Lys857 (corresponding Arg958A2) with Arg converted EphA5 SAM into a SHIP2 binding SAM domain, though the binding was still relatively weak.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The K857R substitution in EphA5 SAM enhanced EphA5 SAM's binding to Odin SAM1 by more than 100-fold.
source: The same substitution also enhanced EphA5 SAM's binding to Odin SAM1 by more than 100-fold (Figure 2H, bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Specific SAM domain-mediated effector binding is required for ligand-induced cell repulsion function of EphA2.
source: We next tested the cellular function of the specific SAM domain-mediated effector association of the EphA2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell biology experiments.

claim: DU145 cells have a low expression level of endogenous EphA2 receptors.
source: DU145 cells, which have a low expression level of endogenous EphA2 receptors, were used to study its ligand-induced inhibition of cell spreading (Barquilla et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012; Miao et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Cells expressing wild-type full-length EphA2 receptor dramatically retracted and became rounded in response to ephrinA1-Fc stimulation.
source: As expected and consistent with the previous reports (Barquilla et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2017), in response to ephrinA1-Fc stimulation, cells expressing the wild-type full-length EphA2 receptor dramatically retracted and became rounded, whereas the negative control cells did not respond to ephrinA1 (Figure 3A and quantified in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and B with supporting citations.

claim: Cells expressing EphA2 delSAM, EphA2 R958K, or EphA2-SAMA5 chimera did not display ephrinA1-induced cell rounding.
source: None of them displayed ephrinA1-induced cell rounding (Figure 3A and B), indicating that the highly specific EphA2 SAM domain-mediated effector association is required for the cell spreading function of EphA2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Overexpressing SHIP2-SAM effectively reversed the cell collapse phenotype caused by ephrinA1 activation of EphA2.
source: The data showed that overexpressing SHIP2-SAM effectively reversed the cell collapse phenotype caused by ephrinA1 activation of EphA2, whereas over-expressing SHIP2-SAM did not lead to any observable changes in the GFP control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that this blocking effect by SHIP2-SAM is EphA2-dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SAMD5 SAM is similar to SHIP2 SAM.
source: Another promising candidate is SAMD5, whose SAM domain is similar to SHIP2 SAM (Figure 4A) and highly expressed in breast cancer cells and mainly cytoplasmic (Lo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A with a supporting citation.

claim: SAMD5 is highly expressed in breast cancer cells and mainly cytoplasmic.
source: Another promising candidate is SAMD5, whose SAM domain is similar to SHIP2 SAM (Figure 4A) and highly expressed in breast cancer cells and mainly cytoplasmic (Lo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: SAMD5 SAM binds to EphA5-8 and EphB1-4 SAM domains with strong affinities.
source: Surprisingly, although the amino acid sequence of SAMD5 SAM can be aligned well (the key binding residues in particular) with the SAM domain sequences of SHIP2 and Odin (Figure 4A, top), SAMD5 bound to EphA5-8 and EphB1-4 SAM domains with strong affinities but only weakly to EphA1/2 SAM domains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SAMD5 binds only weakly to EphA1/2 SAM domains.
source: Surprisingly, although the amino acid sequence of SAMD5 SAM can be aligned well (the key binding residues in particular) with the SAM domain sequences of SHIP2 and Odin (Figure 4A, top), SAMD5 bound to EphA5-8 and EphB1-4 SAM domains with strong affinities but only weakly to EphA1/2 SAM domains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The crystal structure of the EphA5/SAMD5 SAM–SAM complex was solved at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: To delineate the mechanism governing the Eph/SAMD5 interaction, we solved the EphA5/SAMD5 SAM–SAM complex crystal structure at the resolution of 1.9 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Table 1.

claim: EphA5 SAM uses its End-Helix to interact with the Mid-Loop of SAMD5 SAM.
source: Similar to that of EphA2/SHIP2 or EphA6/Odin, EphA5 SAM also uses its End-Helix to interact with the Mid-Loop SAMD5 SAM (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The EphA5/SAMD5 SAM-SAM complex does not contain the π-π stacking observed in the EphA2/SHIP2 and EphA6/Odin complexes.
source: However, their detailed binding mechanisms are quite different. The most prominent difference is that the EphA5/SAMD5 SAM-SAM does not contain the π-π stacking observed in the EphA2/SHIP2 and EphA6/Odin complexes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The EphA5/SAMD5 SAM-SAM interaction is essentially completely mediated by charge–charge and hydrogen bonding interactions.
source: Instead, the EphA5/SAMD5 SAM-SAM is essentially completely mediated by charge–charge and hydrogen bonding interactions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The backbone amine of Gly853A5 forms a strong hydrogen bond with Tyr27SAMD5 sidechain hydroxyl group.
source: The backbone amine of Gly853A5 forms a strong hydrogen bond with Tyr27SAMD5 sidechain hydroxyl group (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Substitution of Tyr27SAMD5 with Phe completely eliminated SAMD5's binding to EphA5.
source: To our surprise, substitution of Tyr27SAMD5 with Phe completely eliminated SAMD5's binding to EphA5 (Figure 5E), indicating the critical role of the Gly853A5-Tyr27SAMD5 hydrogen binding in addition to their steric role.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A Pro residue at the position corresponding to Val852A5 in EphA1/EphA2 SAM domains introduces steric hindrance that perturbs SAMD5 binding.
source: For the EphA1/EphA2 SAM domains, although all the key residues are present, it is noticed that a Pro residue is at the position corresponding to Val852A5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). The sidechain pyrrolidine ring of Pro would introduce steric hindrance with Asp40, and thus may perturb SAMD5 from binding to EphA1/EphA2 SAM domains (Figure 5D), resulting in low affinities (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Replacing Val825 of EphA5 SAM with Pro led to about 10-fold affinity decrease in its binding to SAMD5.
source: Supporting this analysis, replacing Val825 of EphA5 SAM with a Pro led to about 10-fold affinity decrease in its binding to SAMD5.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Substitution of Pro953 in EphA2 with Ala increased its SAMD5 SAM binding by more than 10 fold.
source: Additionally, substitution Pro953 in EphA2 with a smaller residue Ala increased its SAMDs SAM binding by more than 10 fold (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Numerous mutations occur in almost every subtype of Eph genes except for EphB6 in cancer patients.
source: We surveyed the COSMIC cancer somatic mutation database (Forbes et al., 2017; http://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic; a collection of somatic mutations found in cancer patients mainly from large-scale genome sequencing studies) and found that numerous mutations occur in almost every subtype of Eph genes except for EphB6.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to the COSMIC database.

claim: A significant number of mutations in Eph genes fall into the SAM domain regions.
source: A significant number of these mutations fell into the SAM domain regions (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EphA1 R966C, EphA2 R957C, and EphA6 R1014Q mutations totally abolished their binding to SHIP2.
source: As expected, EphA1 R966C, EphA2 R957C, and EphA6 R1014Q mutations (the cation-π forming Arg at α5 helix) totally abolished their binding to SHIP2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: EphA5 G1014S, EphA7 G972V, and EphB3 G974D mutations disrupted their binding to SAMD5.
source: EphA5 G1014S, EphA7 G972V, and EphB3 G974D mutations disrupted their binding to SAMD5 (Figure 6C), further supporting our structural finding that the sidechain-less Gly at the beginning of α5 is critical (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mutations on critical sites such as EphA5 K1018M, EphA6 R1014Q, EphA8 R943H, and EphB1 K926M, A961T all weakened or disrupted their binding to SAMD5.
source: Mutations on other critical sites such as EphA5 K1018M, EphA6 R1014Q, EphA8 R943H, and EphB1 K926M, A961T all weakened or even disrupted their binding to SAMD5 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Every Eph receptor SAM domain adopts stable monomers in solution.
source: We demonstrated that, unlike many other previously characterized polymer forming SAM domains, every Eph receptor SAM domain adopts stable monomers in solution (Harada et al., 2008; Knight et al., 2011; Stapleton et al., 1999; Thanos et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: No SAM–SAM hetero-complexes between Eph SAM domains could form.
source: Additionally, no SAM–SAM hetero-complexes between Eph SAM domains could form (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The SAM domains from EphA2, EphA5, and EphA6 all bind to their effector SAM domain using their respective End-Helix.
source: The structures solved in this study revealed that the SAM domains from EphA2, EphA5, and EphA6 all bind to its effector SAM domain using their respective End-Helix.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural data.

claim: Every Eph SAM domain contains an extremely conserved Mid-Loop.
source: It is noticed that every Eph SAM domain also contains an extremely conserved Mid-Loop (see EphA2/EphA5/EphA6 SAM sequence alignments in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B–D for an example).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B-D.

claim: At least some Eph SAM domains may use their Mid-Loops to bind to the End-Helix of their effector SAM domains.
source: It is compelling to speculate that at least some Eph SAM domains may also use their Mid-Loops to bind to the End-Helix of their effector SAM domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: Many residues in the Mid-Loop regions of Eph SAM domains are found to be mutated in cancer patients.
source: This hypothesis is further supported by the observation that many residues in the Mid-Loop regions of Eph SAM domains are found to be mutated in cancer patients (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The structures of the SAM–SAM complexes can predict three categories of mutations that will likely alter functions of Eph receptors.
source: The structures of the SAM–SAM complexes presented in this work, coupled with amino acid sequence-based analysis, readily predict the following three categories of mutations that will likely alter functions of Eph receptors via changing their SAM domain structures and effector binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural analysis.

claim: Mutations of residues in the folding core or residues playing critical structural roles may impair the overall structure and effector binding of Eph SAM domains.
source: First, mutations of residues in the folding core or residues playing other critical structural roles (e.g. residues highlighted in red in Figure 6A) may impair the overall structure and thus effector binding of Eph SAM domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mutations in the End-Helix region of Eph SAM domains often have defects or total impairments in binding to their effectors.
source: Second, mutations occur in the End-Helix region of Eph SAM domains. This category of Eph SAM domain mutants often has defects or even total impairments in binding to their effectors (Figure 6B and C), and thus are expected to have impaired downstream signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Mutations in the Mid-Loop region of Eph SAM domains may impair their binding to effector SAM domains.
source: Third, mutations occur in the Mid-Loop region of the Eph SAM domains may also impair their binding to effector SAM domain as we mentioned above, although this prediction will need to be verified.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a prediction.

claim: The binding affinities for all Eph SAM-effector SAM interactions are in the submicromolar to micromolar range.
source: The binding affinities for all the interactions reported here are in the submicromolar to micromolar range.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on ITC measurements.

claim: Eph receptors multimerize upon ligand activation, mainly via their extracellular domains.
source: First, Eph receptors are known to multimerize upon ligand activation, mainly via their extracellular domains (Janes et al., 2012; Seiradake et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: SHIP2 can be recruited to the cell membrane via SH2 domain mediated interactions to other cell surface receptors.
source: Second, several studies have revealed that effectors like SHIP2 can be recruited to the cell membrane via SH2 domain mediated interactions to other cell surface receptors (Pesesse et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: There are 110 SAM domain-containing proteins in addition to the 14 Eph receptors and three Eph-binding proteins studied.
